Mr. Speaker, I note that the Minister of Public Works is in the chamber. I would like to ask him if at this time he would give to the House or table in the House the details of the report that he asked for from the members of his staff in the Department of Public Works. Can he advise if he is satisfied with the agreement that was made with Campeau on the Les Terrasses de la Chaudiere project and whether he considers it a good one for the people of Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Judd Buchanan (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, basically the information to which the hon. member makes reference was not in the form of a report. It was a considerable quantity of information relating to Les Terrasses de la Chaudiere project as well as phase three and phase four in Hull and the York Olympia project here in Ottawa. I am still going over some of the details of this information. I am not yet in a position to comment on the final parts of the question.

Does the minister not agree that the taxpayers of Canada are entitled to a full and open inquiry on this contract, particularly in view of its magnitude, as well as the negotiations and circumstances leading to the contract? Can he assure the House that documents and files in his department pertaining to the Terrasses de la Chaudiere deal are not being removed in order to obscure the situation with regard to a subsequent investigation on this project?

Mr. Speaker, to date my investigations have not lead me to believe that there was any wrongdoing, as suggested by the hon. member. Until I am convinced that there was a shred of that type of activity, I do not see the reason or justification for an inquiry.

subsubtopic: MR. JELINEK-NEWSPAPER ARTICLE CONCERNING CONSTITUENCY OFFICE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is the first opportunity I have had to rise on a question of personal privilege pertaining to the article that appeared in Saturday's Globe and Mail concerning my constituency office, as well as to the allusions made on the matter in this House.

subsubtopic: MR. JELINEK-NEWSPAPER ARTICLE CONCERNING CONSTITUENCY OFFICE
speechtext: Shame.

subsubtopic: MR. JELINEK-NEWSPAPER ARTICLE CONCERNING CONSTITUENCY OFFICE
speechtext:
As I read it, Mr. Speaker, that article implied that I was guilty of a misuse of funds voted by this House for the establishment of a riding office. I am accused of conniving with an old age pensioner, my constituency secretary, to pay her money she had not earned. I believe the accusation is as serious in its implication for my reputation as it is erroneous in fact. My constituency office is established in conformity with the spirit as well as the letter of the law; it provides a complete and accessible service to my constituents, and it is similar in location and operation to that of the most effective offices set up by many of my colleagues in this House.
Mr. Speaker, allow me to deal briefly with the specific accusations implying a misuse of funds. The article states that I have committed the government to $200 per month for partial use of a tiny room and kitchen which are so inadequate that interviews must be held in the living room of Miss Pattison, my constituency secretary. This, of course, is false. The fact is that the whole bottom floor is used for riding office purposes. This includes the living room, which is used for interviews, the dining room, which is set up for group meetings or discussions, and a third and smaller area which is used for filing. The kitchen is also available, as an incidental convenience, for coffee. From the $200 per month rent, approximately $45 is deducted for an answering service available to all constituents 24 hours a day, seven days a week, and a phone bill of approximately $15 per month. In addition, Miss Pattison pays all heat and light charges. Far from being a suspicious arrangement, this is as good a value for the taxpayers' money as any, the net result being a saving of roughly 50 per cent to the taxpayer from the government's established allowance of $3,600.
It was stated, as well, that Miss Pattison and the office were not easily accessible to constituents. On the contrary, the office, which is centrally located on a main thoroughfare close to one of the central intersections of the riding, keeps the

November 3, 1976
Privilege-Mr. Jelinek
constituency secretary occupied over six hours a day, six days a week. Certainly, as was stated in the article, Miss Pattison has other community interests in the High Park-Humber Valley area; this only makes her more, not less, suitable as a constituency secretary in helping people with their problems, as her long and extensive community involvements bring her to the heart of local and current affairs.
As for the charge that she refers many problems to my office here in Ottawa, the reasons for this must be obvious to everyone except perhaps the irresponsible Globe and Mail reporter who authored this slanderous article. It is true that the office does not have a sign, because I believe the zoning bylaws do not permit one, and as a result both the address and phone number are listed on a great number of mailings that go from my office to every household in the constituency.
The writer of the article makes much of the fact that my party's constituency president has never been to the riding office. He never has, because I take great pains not to use the office for partisan purposes. All executive meetings and party functions are held elsewhere, as I am sure they are with most members, for a constituency office is not the place to advertise or play party politics. One must wonder how a once reputable newspaper like the Globe and Mail could stoop to such low levels of yellow journalism by utilizing a large portion of its front page with a story so misleading and erroneous.
In any event, I believe the article was so full of half-truths, innuendoes and outright lies that it constitutes a malicious and slanderous attack on my conduct as a member of parliament. I also believe that I would be fully justified in proposing a motion to send this matter to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections so that the mechanics of assembling this vicious and unsubstantiated attack on the character of a member of parliament could be exposed. However, I do not wish to take the further time of the House on this subject matter; and, being aware of suggestions in some of the procedural authorities that libel and slander should be dealt with by the courts, I have instructed my lawyers to proceed accordingly on that basis.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. JELINEK-NEWSPAPER ARTICLE CONCERNING CONSTITUENCY OFFICE
speechtext:
Order, please. I have no difficulty concluding, as I have on numerous occasions in the past, that the hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley (Mr. Jelinek) has raised what he considers to be a grievance in respect of the reporting of his activities. subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REGULATE INTEREST ON JUDGMENT DEBTS AND AMEND CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last night when 1 called it ten o'clock I was saying that although we on this side were giving agreement to the principle of this
{Mr. Goodale.]
bill, it was necessary to find fault with the lack of consultation with consumer groups and with the absence of specific rates and other details which the minister says will be spelled out in the regulations.
I want to deal for a moment today with the unwarranted credit charge rate, which rate is not stated in the bill. It seems that the minister wants to leave the determination of the unwarranted rate to the courts and that in each case it will be determined on the merits of the particular case. This, of course, will clog up the courts. It will put the burden of proof on the lender, which is a complete change from the rule of law in this country whereby one is innocent until proven guilty. Here, the lender will be assumed guilty until he can prove himself innocent. There will be a serious trend here. The tendency of this rule will be to restrict the making of loans to good risks. Further, it will restrict the rights of the bad risks and improve the chance of business going to the loan sharks.
We have always had a matter of choice in our life in Canada, bad as the choice might be. For example, a tenant might prefer to pay a higher rate of interest than is allowed in order to avoid a court order eviction. The minister, in his remarks, referred to the unwarranted rate and said that when the ceiling rates for small loans were lower than prevailing credit market rates, lenders had refused to grant small loans, forcing higher risk borrowers to seek funds from loan sharks. Mr. Speaker, nothing he is proposing now is going to change that situation.
Further on, the minister said interest rates would be set "according to the cost of funds and the risks involved in a particular transaction." This, of course, will be the defence in court. The minister says that if a borrower, after seeking sound professional advice, believes that the rate he is being charged is too high, he can choose to apply to a court for a review of the credit charge and the court will determine whether or not the rate is warranted. But why not make such a determination beforehand instead of going through the courts after the fact? I believe the lender has a right to choose the risks he wishes to accept, and the likelihood is that the source of funds will be dried up to the disadvantage of the very people the minister seems to wish to help.
I turn now to the computation of interest on sums deposited. The minister intends to require the interest calculation to be made on a daily basis. This seems a good idea and I am sure people whose savings vary from day to day will agree with it. However, on examination it becomes evident that this would impose a penalty on steady savers, those who deposit every month, who do not need computation of interest on a daily basis but who will be asked to share in the cost of daily calculation in order to benefit other depositors.
I see a number of other specific problems arising. An administrator is to be appointed. Heaven knows, Mr. Speaker, there are already enough senior bureaucrats around Ottawa. The powers to be given him are enormous. For example, he will be permitted to enter any premises at any time to conduct
November 3, 1976

audits, seize records, and so on. All this will involve huge cost to the taxpayer. In addition, there are, of course, many clauses in the bill which impose additional obligations on lenders, the costs of which obviously will be passed on to the borrowers.
One noteworthy-I might say "notorious"-feature of the legislation as it affects lenders is that a payment made on a loan is deemed to have been made on the day it is sent by mail. In Canada today, mail sometimes takes weeks to arrive. No exemption is provided in the case of disruption of the postal service, and I suggest that lenders are being made subject to a heavy penalty which is particularly serious when large sums are paid on a Friday after banking hours.
It might be said that I am pitying the lenders too much and that lenders can take care of themselves. However, I would point out that lenders, in the main, are only trustees of funds belonging to small depositors. Union funds are used to make loans. Funds entrusted to trust companies for the care of widows and orphans are similarly used. Life insurance companies are, after all, investing the funds of millions of Canadians. Even the banks, the so-called beasts of the financial world, number many thousands of Canadians among their shareholders.
I want to say a word now about loan-sharking. The minister told us last week that he wanted to help our police forces to fight the ever-increasing crime of loan-sharking. That is a very fine objective. But he did not tell us what loan-sharking is, and the details given in the bill are illusive if not invisible. Perhaps a better picture will emerge when the regulations are forthcoming, but as things stand we are being asked to pass the bill as presented.
In his speech the minister told us the government had not been able to end the activities of loan sharks, and that any rate today was a legal rate. We might ask ourselves why the government did not move effectively into this area during the past 14 years, and why they have not been able to define an appropriate rate. In fact, only the ceilings on small loan interest rates have been removed. We know the industry will get along somehow, no matter what restrictions the government may impose. But why cannot the minister tell us what the criminal rate under this bill is to be?
I am concernced about the methods used by loan sharks to enforce their claims. Certainly, the description of those methods is awful. But tactics of this kind are already illegal-one cannot go around threatening people or beating up people in Canada today. I do not think the minister is correct when he says that the provisions he is putting forward in this respect will really help the police.
The minister did refer to the "criminal rate" in the course of his remarks and said the bill would establish one. But there is no mention of such a rate in the measure before us. He said he would be clear and concise, and that the rate would be of great value to those launching criminal prosecutions. He told us the level would be set well above the rate normally charged in the market. Well, what is it? Evidence given in committee during examination of tfye Small Loans Act would indicate that the warranted rate is something like 80 per cent. Does this mean
Protection of Borrowers and Depositors that the criminal rate will be 150 per cent or 200 per cent? We are not told, yet there is a penalty clause, clause 38, which sets out in great detail the penalties which can be imposed under the act.
On the subject of tax refund discounting, the minister said such discounting was "clearly an unscrupulous practice". Well, the government has the solution to this problem in its own hands. The only reason for which a person needs to get his tax refund discounted is that he cannot get his money from the government. I suggest there is no difference between a man borrowing on the strength of a promise to pay from the government in the shape of a future tax rebate, and a man borrowing on the strength of a Canadian bond. I read in a newspaper yesterday that certain bonds issued by the government of Canada are being quoted at a discount rate of 72 per cent of their value. That is a fairly normal figure. The most infamous case is that of the 3 per cent perpetuals which are being discounted at $47.
The government has the ability to eliminate this problem entirely. It could accept an application from Canadians in, let us say, November to have an interim calculation made of the amount of tax they will have to pay and they could get a refund. The government has lots of clerical capacity, especially in this day of computers, and so on, to make this calculation. The government makes deductions from wages on the basis of a full year's work. We all know that particularly those workers who suffer hardship and who need to borrow money do not work for a full year. Therefore, I suggest the government owes it to them to make interim calculations so as to eliminate this particular problem.
The minister has been insistent on knowing what suggestions we on this side would make in view of the fact that we are not in agreement with all of his proposals. 1 have listed a few for the minister and will give them to him now, and no doubt we will be discussing them in committee. First of all, the government has it within its power to control to some degree rates of interest by controlling the rate of inflation. Naturally, as long as the inflation rate remains as high as it is, interest rates are not going to be any lower. We recommend that the government regulate this industry as it does others, but not compete as it does in other fields. We suggest that clear rules are necessary. However, apart from the principles laid out, this bill gives us no clear rules whatever and puts far too much power in the hands of the ministry.
A government that was concerned could regulate in order to require retailers to provide credit at certain rates on all sales that they make on credit. That is the kind of regulatory device that would not require that the government be directly involved. The government should allow the marketplace to set rates; that is, to encourage competition. That, as we have seen in other fields, is the most effective way of providing properly priced services for Canadians.
I have already mentioned the streamlining of the tax system which would eliminate the need for tax refund discounting. It

November 3, 1976
Protection of Borrowers and Depositors
is obvious that banks and trust companies now compete vigorously to obtain depositors' business. All one has to do is look around in January or February of any year to see the many different rates offered on registered retirement savings plans. Just at the moment, in the present general business climate there is a lot of investment money and plenty of competition for borrowers in the money market. If rates are controlled too much, then credit will not be available to all those who need it, and that is not what the government says it wants.
Finally, on Monday the minister said that he hoped I would be on the committee to help with amendments. All I can say is that I hope the minister is not just being naive, because it has been my experience, Mr. Speaker, during my four years in this House that usually the government does not accept amendments easily, even though in the case of one specific bill in the last session the government approved 54 amendments. Even although the Globe and Mail has reported the minister as saying that this in no way is the final form of the bill, I will have to be convinced in committee that the minister is sincere in his wish to have this bill amended. I have never felt that it was the opposition's job to perfect government's legislation and to give the government credit for producing a good bill. However, I shall be in attendance in the committee, and I hope that we will get fuller information at that time so that for the benefit of the borrowers of Canada we can perfect this bill.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thought that Bill C-16 would provide me with an opportunity to congratulate the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Abbott) and wish him every success. But having read Bill C-16, all I can do is congratulate the minister on his appointment and wish him no success in regard to the passage of this bill. He has failed miserably and dismally in regard to solving the problem of exorbitant interest rates, commonly called loan-sharking and he has not dealt with excessive interest rates. I can appreciate the problem the minister faced. He is a former corporation counsel, and when he was appointed to this position he had to decide whether he would be an advocate for the corporate boards or whether he would be an advocate for consumers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am just giving my interpretation of the problem the minister had. He has the background of a corporation counsel. To me, he must have had a problem deciding whether he would be an advocate for the corporate boards or whether he would be a consumer advocate. Having

read the bill, I realize that he opted for being the advocate of the corporate boards.
This is a bill of least resistance to the credit institutions, with little or no protection to borrowers. It is what is known as a candy-floss bill-all sweetness and no substance. I direct the minister's attention to the title of the bill. He has the nerve to call it the borrowers and depositors protection bill. What protection does it give the borrower? What protection does it give the depositor? He should have called the bill the lenders and loan sharks protection bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REGULATE INTEREST ON JUDGMENT DEBTS AND AMEND CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext: Obviously you have not read the bill.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REGULATE INTEREST ON JUDGMENT DEBTS AND AMEND CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext:
The main principle enunciated in the bill, namely, that of protecting the Canadian borrower from loansharking and excessive interest rates, will not succeed because it is based on two approaches-on self-policing by credit institutions, and on comparative competition on the money marketplace. These approaches are like asking a starving cannibal to stop eating the missionary. It is like asking the loan sharks to start acting like Sister Theresa. The main principle is wrong and unworkable. It is a surrender to the credit institutions and a rejection of the necessity for basic protection for the borrower, and more especially for people of low income.
All members of the House can quickly and readily agree with the other three principles which the minister outlined in his speech: (a) to provide information with regard to credit and deposit dealings; (b) to eliminate complexities and confusion in the credit field; (c) to regularize and rationalize credit legislation. May I remind Your Honour and all members of the House that these other corrective measures are the direct result of the chicanery, greed and duplicitous dealings of credit institutions. These dealings have required provincial legislation to protect the borrower against lenders, and now we are introducing federal legislation.
Returning to the main principles of the legislation put forward by the minister, protection of the Canadian borrower from loan-sharking and excessive interest rates by imposing self-policing on credit institutions and comparative competition in the money market, if the minister had made the same speech as the hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray), I would be tempted to agree with him. The hon. member for Windsor West cut right into the heart of the problem when he asked whether this measure deals in the best way with loansharking and excessive interest rates. The substance of his speech indicates it does not.
It is striking that the hon. member for Windsor West makes far better speeches now that he is out of the cabinet. I suppose the reason is that he can now tell it the way it is. The hon. member for Windsor West reminded the minister of the Liberal policy and program in the 1974 election when they put forward the consumer protection package. The hon. member enumerated some of those principles but he omitted two main parts of the Liberal program. I shall point them out to hon.
November 3, 1976

members because I am sure they would like to have their memories refreshed.
In the 1974 election campaign, the Liberal party said that it would have a loan insurance scheme for low-paid workers who could not establish a credit rating. Second, the Liberal party said it would have consumer-help storefront offices the number of which would be increased to 20 by the end of 1974. The hon. member for Windsor West did not mention these two main items in the Liberal program. The reason is that the Liberals do not have them. They have established no storefront credit counselling offices to help people who are borrowing money and to make them aware of interest rates and some of the nefarious schemes of credit institutions. More importantly, the Liberal party has not adopted the other principle, that is, loan insurance for people with low incomes who have difficulty obtaining loans.
The minister said he is going to protect people against loan-sharking and excessive interest rates by having credit institutions police themselves. Have hon. members ever heard of such an approach for protecting borrowers from loan-sharking and excessive interest rates? The government is asking the very people who are guilty of these practices to police themselves in order to protect the borrower. The minister is relying on those credit institutions.
Let me tell the House about banks. What is the practice of banks with regard to paying interest on deposits? Twice a year they pay interest on the lowest minimum deposit in depositors' accounts. The banks talk about red convertible loans in times of inflation. The minister is asking these institutions to police themselves in order to protect the borrower. Let us consider the front-end loading charges and service charges, the costs, the credit reports, the prepayment charges and the misleading advertising as to rates of interest of finance companies. Let us consider the kickbacks car dealers receive for turning over credit notes to finance companies. These are the finance companies we are asking to police themselves in order to protect the borrower against loan-sharking and excessive interest rates.
By exhortations and warnings, the government is going to ask loan sharks to lower their interest rates. The government is going to do this in the face of recent releases by the minister and a speech by him saying that loan sharks charge in excess of 1,000 per cent to borrowers who are disadvantaged and must seek high-risk loans. The minister suggests a rate of seven times the prime rate. The prime rate for loans in Canada at the moment is 10 per cent, so the minister is saying that as long as lenders charge a rate less than 70 per cent or 75 per cent, they are not charging the criminal rate.
The minister is asking these people to police themselves with regard to loan-sharking and charging excessive interest rates. Can we rely on bank officials, finance companies and loan sharks to protect the borrower? The answer is no. I am surprised at the naivety of the minister in thinking that these groups are capable of self-policing. Their past practices have forced the minister to write into legislation the need to inform and protect the public with regard to information on credit and
Protection of Borrowers and Depositors deposit dealings and the need to define strict and uniform rules to protect borrowers and depositors respecting effective rates of interest. This is why relying on credit institutions to police themselves will not work.
With regard to the second principle the minister has enunciated, competition in the money market, the minister feels that by some strange osmosis we are going to have competition in the money market. We have never had real competition in the money market. Bank rates are exactly the same for their three different types of loans. With regard to finance companies, they are practically the same, and loan sharks do not use competitive rates. There has never been any real competition in the money market. Any competition has been on a service basis only, never on an interest rate basis. The result has been slick advertisements by financial institutions which say, "We are your friendly finance company", or, "Don't borrow money needlessly". For a former member, a great hockey player and a great coach, Red Kelly, to advertise on behalf of Beneficial Finance does not do him or advertising ethics any credit.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REGULATE INTEREST ON JUDGMENT DEBTS AND AMEND CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext: It puts money in the bank.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REGULATE INTEREST ON JUDGMENT DEBTS AND AMEND CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext:
It is quite true that it puts money in the banks and finance companies, but we must remember that all this advertising gimmickry is a cost factor to be included in interest rates. Competition has been illusory or non-existent. What is the defence of the minister? He says that if a person has been overcharged, he can take court action or default on his payments and force the lender to sue him. What bravado by the minister! Can hon. members imagine a low income worker having sufficient bravado to say, "Let them sue me; let them take me to court and I will prove that they have charged excessive interest rates"? What would be the result? In the first instance, it would be no contest because of reluctance by the borrower to sue and because of the legal costs involved. Second, the possibility or probability of blacklisting or blackballing the borrower by lenders in the future would be very real. The third result is the probable action by these institutions in respect of contracting-out provisions in the loan agreement.
We have had experience with regard to contracting-out and warranties given by companies concerning goods. We have had contracting-out with regard to leases under the landlord and tenant act. The law says that the landlord shall not unreasonably withhold consent to transfer, but we have found leases which contain clauses in respect of contracting-out. We will find the same thing with loan agreements and credit applications. I am sure the minister will jump quickly to the defence in this respect and say he has a provision within the act which will prevent contracting-out.
There is a very practical problem with regard to contracting-out. I can see the wording that will be in the agreement. The borrower will say he is satisfied and accepts the interest rate therein and will acknowledge that the "Meet 'em and

November 3, 1976
Protection of Borrowers and Depositors
Cheat 'em" credit company has taken into account all the provisions and criteria set forth in the protection of borrowers and depositors act and he hereby waives his right to independent advice and any or all legal proceedings. That is an example of the typical contracting provision that we will find. In any contract we will find that provision. It will contain the amount of the loan, the interest chargeable, and the payment date.
The minister says that in his legislation, in order for the borrower to use such an instrument as a defence, or if the company is to use it, the company shall give 15 days' notice if the action is to be commenced. I say that provision will be part and parcel of the contract. Under the ordinary rules of evidence, if the borrower is to prove excessive rates he will have to file the agreement in order to show the terms of the contract, and by putting that provision in he is consenting to the terms of the contract and to the contracting-out clause and is thereby limited in his defence.
We have had experience with regard to the unconscionable transactions act of Ontario. We know there have been very few actions under that act and very few successes. The reason is that the people who draw up these contracts consider all the possible defences of the borrower and tighten the contract to the point where the borrower has little or no hope of success when he goes to court. We will have the same results in respect of any action a borrower may take with regard to excessive interest rates. For these reasons, my colleagues and I think the bill is a sham and constitutes a surrender to the credit institutions.
Let me deal with one final argument the minister set forth in his press release. The argument goes like this: the credit institutions have a certain investment in dollars. They are in the business of making a profit. I do not use the word "reasonable", because they make unconscionable profits. If they cannot make these profits in the credit field, they will go elsewhere to invest their moneys, and what a tragedy would befall the poor, defenceless borrowers: this is the argument of the minister. It is much like the argument of the little boy who had a ball and said, "If you don't let me play the game my way, I will take my ball and go home".
We have had similar experience in the building field. In recent months builders have said they do not like the economic and taxation climate in Canada and therefore they will go to the south. They have gone to the United States to invest in real estate and building to the tune of $l'/2 billion to date. This is the type of attitude the builders have, and it is the type of attitude the minister thinks the credit institutions will take, that is: if you do not let me make all the profits that are obtainable, I will not invest in the field and the poor people will suffer.
Surely the making of a reasonable profit should be the basis of credit lending in Canada. It should not be an unconscionable profit; it should not be usury. How much is enough? When one sees the profits that the various finance companies and loan sharks make, it is evident that they are more than enough. There is a social responsibility on the credit institutions to use the moneys of Canadian depositors and investors

to the fair advantage of both borrower and lender. There is a biblical proverb to the effect that the borrower is the servant of the lender. In Canada, the borrower is becoming the slave of the lender. I remember George Bernard Shaw in one of his books saying that the rich man will do anything for the poor man except to get off his back and keep his hands out of the poor man's pocket.
Members of the New Democratic Party have a different approach to the problems of excessive interest rates and loansharking. We would replace the approach of the minister, of self-policing and the competitive money market aspect with four things. First, we would institute the requirement of loan insurance for the borrower. Second, we would impose ceilings on loan amounts and interest rates. Third, we would have a massive program of budget counselling in schools, churches, social agencies and community centres to teach budget counselling. Fourth, we would appoint a credit ombudsman to protect the borrower and to license, regulate and control the lender by use of court action by the ombudsman, by the use of class actions and by the use of cease and desist orders and consent orders.
Let me speak briefly on the four principles we would adopt. First, the requirement of loan insurance would be a cost factor in determining the rate of interest. This is not new. As I reminded the minister, this was part of the Liberal program in 1974. I shall read this, Mr. Speaker:
-loan insurance scheme for low-paid workers who cannot establish a credit rating.
This is what the Liberals said they would do in 1974, and it is what they are not doing in 1976. The federal government uses loan insurance in a variety of ways. First, it uses it in the mortgage field; all NHA mortgages and CMHC direct loan mortgages and AHOP mortgages have insurance. The purchaser pays a premium of 1 per cent of the loan. It has been a success with regard to default in payments by the borrowers. It is what is known as "spread the risk". The federal government uses it in respect of student loans, small business loans, farmers' loans, and fishermen's loans-to protect whom: to protect the banks and other institutions with regard to default by a student, fisherman or farmer.
The government is prepared to protect the banks against default by the borrower. The government is prepared to protect multinational companies such as International Nickel when loans are given by the Export Development Bank to stimulate exports. When loans are given by the Export Development Bank to stimulate exports, the government says to International Nickel, "We will provide insurance against a company in any other country defaulting on its payments". The government is assuring payment to the multinational corporations.
The final insurance aspect is deposit insurance, that is, to protect bank depositors from the bankruptcy or failure of a bank. Surely, .if we can protect the banks against default by borrowers, we can give the borrower some protection against
November 3, 1976

the lender. At this stage, the banks, some finance companies and credit unions use a limited form of loan insurance in case of the death of a borrower. If a borrower dies, the loan is paid up. There is no reason why we cannot adopt loan insurance, especially for low income workers. If that is the case, how does it affect the problem of loan-sharking and excessive interest rates? It spreads the risk, which is the principle of insurance, and it should, and would, reduce high interest rates because it would sweep away the argument of the banks, the finance companies and the loan sharks regarding high-risk loans.
It would result in a reasonable return to the lender and a reasonable and fair chance of repayment by the borrower. It would rid us of the problem of determining the unwarranted rate or the criminal rate, and it would rid us of loan sharks.
You, Mr. Speaker, have the right to ask what happens if the borrower does not pay loan insurance. It is obvious that no further loans would be made to him. This is the practice with regard to student loans. A constituent of mine who went to university back in 1972 and borrowed money for it, quit the university in 1974 and did not pay back his student loan. In 1976 he wanted to go back to university to take a course and he applied for a student loan. He was advised by the administrator of the fund in Ottawa that he could not get a loan because he had already an outstanding loan. Surely that principle should apply to borrowers under this act, because no person has the inalienable right to borrow. Before a person borrows, he must establish need and he must establish himself with regard to the risk; he must indicate a payment record. In those circumstances, the borrower would try his utmost to repay the loan. I am amazed at the number of people who go to finance companies and are most anxious to maintain their credit rating. They try their darndest to keep up the payments.
If we had loan insurance, we would have no multiplicity of loans with finance companies. It is rather sad to have people come into my constituency office with credit problems. When you ask what credit they have outstanding, you find they have loans with different finance companies, sometimes three or four of them. If we had loan insurance we would not have such a multiplicity of loans with different finance companies. In certain circumstances we could impose a requirement on a borrower to take budget counselling when necessary.
With regard to the second proposition put forward by the NDP for the imposition of ceilings on loans and on interest rates, we agree with the loan amounts imposed by the Consumers' Association of Canada of $7,500 plus a consumer price index adjustment. We have the same approach with regard to AHOP loans. Those loans are adjusted from time to time and there is no reason why a ceiling of $7,500 cannot be imposed with a consumer price index adjustment.
I have heard it said by the minister and by some members of the House that the Small Loans Act did not work. It is the intention of the minister to rescind the Small Loans Act. The reason the act did not work was that it was circumvented by the lenders. What would happen if a person went to a credit institution? They had a limit of $1,500 on loans. A person would asked for a loan of $1,000 and the credit institution
Protection of Borrowers and Depositors would say to him; "No, we will not lend you $1,000"-the reason being that $1,000 would bring low interest rates-"but we will lend you $1,600, $100 over the limit of $1,500, and we will charge you 25 per cent". That is the reason the Small Loans Act did not serve the purpose for which it was intended. It was circumvented, not by the borrower but more especially by the lender. All that had to be done was to adjust the loan limits under the Small Loans Act and in some cases adjust the interest rates. It makes no sense to rescind the Small Loans Act and say it did not work, we know it was circumvented by the lending institutions; let us make no mistake about it.
The practice of credit institutions is to impose different loan interest rates on different customers. But the banks have different types of loans. They have business loans, on which they usually charge a prime rate of about 10 per cent, they have consumer loans at 13 per cent and 14 per cent, and they have mortgage loans which are at the moment 11 Vi per cent, and farm improvement loans which are practically the same, 11V2 per cent. Banks serve a business community and the middle and upper classes, but they have limits on the amount of the loan and limits on the interest rate.
Finance companies deal in consumer loans and they have limits on the amount of the loan and on the interest rates, and usually the interest rates vary from 24 per cent to 33 per cent. They serve the low income and the lower middle income people who have a basic fear of the banks and therefore go to the finance companies. Then there are the loan sharks who impose their own rates. According to the minister, some of those rates are 1,000 per cent. They impose them on the poor and disadvantaged. Some might say that those are not loan limits or limits on the interest rates, but they are market interest rates. I rather doubt that there is any competition with regard to the market interest rate, because banks get the money from the depositors and lend it out at the highest rate they can obtain. There may be a little competition, but not much. What do finance companies do? They borrow from banks and add on to what they pay to the banks to make their profit.
Mr. Speaker, if the minister is worried about the competitive rates of the banks, all he has to do is use them and add a reasonable rate of return by banks, finance companies and loan sharks. When the former finance spokesman for the Conservative party sat on the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs in 1967, he knew that there was a formula for interest rates which was used for CMHC mortgages. It was the rate of return on Canada savings bonds, plus an adjustment of W2 per cent or 2 per cent. So there is no reason the minister cannot use the basic prime rate imposed by the banks and add a reasonable rate of return. Anything beyond that is unwarranted, unjustified and criminal.
I am rather impressed with the minister, Mr. Speaker, because I think he is morally a very fine gentleman. I find it morally reprehensible, however, that he puts in his press release a suggestion of seven times the basic interest rate to determine the warranted rate.

November 3, 1976
Protection of Borrowers and Depositors

Thank you, Mr. Speaker, and I thank my colleagues. 1 shall not take more than five minutes. The New Democratic Party's proposition is a far better approach than that of the minister, that of self-policing in the competition of the money marketplace. We would have a massive program of budget counselling, but not the type the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) was worried about yesterday. Surely not every borrower needs to take a course in budget counselling. We say this should be instituted in the schools, community centres, credit unions and churches so that people would get a good idea of how budget counselling works.
We propose the appointment of a credit ombudsman, separate and apart from the minister. I am not the least impressed by the appointment of an administrator who would be an arm of the minister and an arm of the credit institutions and would afford little or no protection to the borrower. I propose a credit ombudsman to license lenders, impose cease and desist orders, consent orders and to put some strength into this matter.
Mr. Speaker, I have to give some credit to the minister on the matter of interest on bank deposits, but surely there should be a daily interest rate instead of the present practice where banks give interest on the lowest minimum balance every month, payable twice a year. I notice many of the credit institutions have agreed to this proposal, and I was surprised to hear some members speaking on behalf of the banks trying to make out that this is a difficult system. Many of the institutions are doing it already, so it is no problem.
With regard to the privilege of the repayment of mortgage loans at 10 per cent on the anniversary of the interest payment for the first year, 10 per cent on the principal payment of the second year, and all or any on the anniversary of the third year on payment of three months' interest, I find this a very interesting provision. I should like to know how many people with CMHC mortgages, and how many with NHA mortgages-which are government insured-have taken advantage of that privilege.
Members might be interested to know that on a $50,000 mortgage, at the current interest rate of 11-% per cent for a period of 25 years, which is how long it takes the average person to pay off a mortgage, the monthly payment of princi-

pal and interest is $498.54. After 25 years the mortgagee has paid, in principal and interest, a total of $143,562. I am not too impressed with that "privilege" clause, Mr. Speaker; it is just a sop. If I were minister of consumer and corporate affairs I would be more interested in bringing down the interest rate so that people who buy a home are given a reasonable chance, with reasonable payments, to pay it off in a reasonable time.
Finally, I say this bill has little to commend it. The saying, "Neither a lender nor a borrower be" should be, "Never a borrower be, under the provisions of this bill." The minister made a tragic mistake when he insisted on calling the bill the borrowers and depositors protection act. To be honest, he ought to have called it the lenders and loan sharks protection act. I congratulate him on his appointment, wish him no success with passage of the bill, and give him this advice, "Consult the people in the department and return to this House with a bill of which you and we can be proud, a bill which will protect borrowers fairly and will limit the gouging of lenders."

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always pleasant to rise after the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) has spoken in this House. As usual, he presented his own version of Alice in Wonderland and, in suggesting what he did, went wandering about in the clouds. I should think we would be in general agreement with the purported aims of this bill. No one is compelled to be a borrower, Mr. Speaker. Those who borrow today perform a conscious act. They know that they have not got the money to buy what they want, so they borrow to take a trip, to go on holiday, and so on. They even borrow money to go to the races. People borrow money for all sorts of foolish pleasures. An examination of the history of credit will show, I think, that the number of borrowings which are justified and not justified is about the same.
To say that everything is loaded on the side of the lender is wrong. 1 admit that some unconscionable lenders operate on the fringe of credit granting. But there are just as many, if not more, unconscionable borrowers-skippers, people who borrow with no intention of repaying. They are drifters, grafters, people who abscond with goods originally bought on time. They are dishonest, and what they do is no better and no worse than what the unconscionable lender does.
From time to time legislation like the Small Loans Act and the Interest Act has appeared on our statute books but has gone by the boards. These laws are out of date because inflation has been allowed to take such a free run in the economy and the amounts recited in those acts are no longer relevant. Now the government of Canada has come forward with a bill which I say is largely cosmetic. It acts as if it has sole responsibility in this field. Actually, statutes passed by the provinces, particularly by Ontario and Alberta, have covered most of this ground for 20 years. Those provincial laws are still adequate.
Protection of Borrowers and Depositors
Let me illustrate my experience with the Alberta legislation. I remember, as solicitor for a department store, participating in negotiations with the then attorney general as to terms which would be included when any document, conditional sales agreement or chattel mortgage evidenced the purchase of big-ticket items. Provisions in provincial laws are better, I think, than the ones contained in this bill. Yesterday I asked the minister a question to which he failed to reply. I will ask it again: Does he believe that this legislation will override pertinent legislation existing in almost all provinces and covering property and civil rights? Have we developed another version of the theory that father knows best, or big brother knows best? Does the minister believe that the legislation is superior to and overrides, for example, the credit and loan agreements act of Alberta which came into force in about 1955? I invite the minister and his officials to read what is meant by time sale agreements.
Bill C-16 purports, with a great deal of horn-blowing, to represent itself as the new charter for those buying on time. Nothing could be further from the truth. Both the Alberta and the Ontario laws have for many years required all this disclosure. Actually, provincial disclosure requirements are more honest than those proposed by the minister or by his advisers who may have put certain words in his mouth, words which 1 think he may want to reconsider. I refer to the minister's words as reported at the foot of page 635 of Hansard for November 1:
It is now possible for lenders to stack a variety of other charges on top of the quoted cost of borrowing. Insurance premiums, various administrative charges, legal costs, registration costs and the like are very often charged to the consumer and, in most cases, excluded from the calculation of the cost of borrowing. As a result, the consumer is not apprised of the real interest burden that he actually has to carry.
I repeat what I said previously, the minister is lumping together apples, oranges, cherries, bananas and other things in the same basket. The point is that provincial legislation in Alberta and other provinces provides that if a big-ticket item, such as furniture, is sold pursuant to a conditional sales contract or a chattel mortgage, such document, to be enforceable, must be registered. Usually it is registered at the courthouse, at a rate set by the provinces which depends on a sliding scale, the amount of the purchase, and so on. That is part of the cost of borrowing.
Another cost is that of insurance. It is there for the protection of the borrower in the event that he or she should die and the family should be faced with a claim. Remember, under a time contract or chattel mortgage the lender or vendor is not limited to repossessing the goods. There is an obligation to repay the money, at the election of the lender or vendor. There could be an unpaid balance, under a conditional sales agreement, of many thousands of dollars for an automobile, tractor or combine.
I am sure that a farmer purchasing a combine today costing thousands of dollars would be most happy to have a few dollars of insurance costs that guarantee his estate would be protected

Protection of Borrowers and Depositors from any unpaid balance should he die before completing the payments under the contract. That is only sensible. There are other legitimate charges, such as the cost of doing business, and legal costs. After all, the loan is not for the sole benefit of the lender; it is the borrower who wants to borrow the money. I am sorry that the minister left to attend a meeting, but I would like, from his parliamentary secretary or his officials, clarification of this part of the minister's remarks on Monday afternoon.
Charges such as insurance, registration charges and legal costs are certainly costs of borrowing. No one denies that. However, to then say that was the real rate of interest, in other words, that legal costs, insurance costs and registration costs are really interest costs, is poppycock. It is misleading. For a person concerned with the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs it is totally irresponsible to make such a statement in the House.
I wish to deal with the three main goals of the minister. I am going to comment on the first two. I quote the minister:
The first is to impose uniformity in the practices used for the calculation, crediting and description of interest on all those who take deposits from or make loans to consumers in Canada, and to require a full, uniform and comprehensible disclosure system so that the consumer, before he enters into a deposit or borrowing transaction, will know all his rights and the obligations he will have to bear.
Will this legislation override the credit and loans agreement act of 1967 of the province of Alberta, should it vary in any pertinent detail, or the consumer protection act, Revised Statutes of Ontario, 1970, particularly regulation No. 128 which details it? It may be that the regulations which will form a great part of Bill C-16-and we have seen but the tip of the iceberg-will be apparent in the legislation of some of the provinces. I suggest there may be a real battle. Somehow or other, Big Brother has said we are going to pass an act in this House of Commons in a jurisdiction that is undeniably that of the provinces and has been for well over a century. The provinces will all have to line up, touch their forelocks, bend the knee and say that the federal legislation is going to override their legislation, and they will conform.
If it is the desire to establish uniformity, let the minister say that he and his officials are going to convince the appropriate ministries in the provincial governments to establish uniform legislation. That would be a positive act, and I would agree with it. However, to say that this bill will establish such uniformity is sheer poppycock. I again quote the minister:
The second goal is to facilitate the proper functioning of the market by encouraging more vigorous competition and providing the consumer both with protection and with the right of civil recourse.
We will see whether there is greater accessibility of credit for potential borrowers. We will see whether there will be meaningful civil recourse against unconscionable contracts.
Thirdly, this bill will establish a clear and easily provable criminal offence to act as a strong deterrent to the cancer of loan-sharking that has spread throughout this country.
Why not amend the Criminal Code, if loan-sharking should be a criminal offence-and it is not at the present time. We have bills like Bill C-83, of non-lamented fame, of the last

session. Loan-sharking could have been described in that bill and made part of the criminal law, something the minister is trying to do under this law. There is one thing about a lot of this regulation and the so-called attempts to increase competition by increasing regulations and making it more difficult for lenders to operate. There is something that does not click in the bureaucratic mind. Every regulation requiring an act on behalf of a manufacturer, distributor, supplier, merchant, lender, or what-have-you, results in a cost. Who pays it? The consumer-the very person this legislation is alleged to benefit.
Take the banks and the trust companies which are already covered by a great deal of legislation, inspection and practice, and impose further requirements. Has any one of the people who talk about the daily calculation of interest determined how much it costs to calculate that interest, verify it and balance the books? Many years ago, for some two years I exercised what little grey matter I had-

speechtext: It's all gone now.

speechtext:
It became honed-in very well, compared to the stuff you people put out. I worked on interest rates as a bank clerk. Hon. members may remind me how long it used to take to figure that out manually some 35 years ago. I am reminded of the hours and the days and the cost involved in calculating interest; and in those days it was 2'/i per cent on savings accounts. I remember, also, calculating interest at IVi per cent on savings accounts. That was done on the minimum quarterly balance, as I recall it. Later, the calculation was made on the basis of the minimum monthly balance. So I can tell hon. members just what is involved in the cost of calculating interest payments, bearing in mind the far greater volume and complexity of savings accounts today. We say to the banks and to the trust companies, "Just calculate this interest on a daily basis." Well, perhaps they will calculate interest on loans on a daily basis. Let us see, then, if the smile goes on the other side of the face. This is a two-edged sword.
If costs for the operation of savings accounts go up because of the requirements of this bill, all that will happen is that the interest spread will have to be widened. In other words, the interest rate will have to be lowered. It is not the banks which are going to pay for this. Moreover, if there is a decline in profits, the federal treasury will suffer because 50 per cent of this additional expenditure will be deductible from taxable income. Thus, in the end, the requirement could be self-defeating; I think the bottom-line figures on the balance sheet would be zero or something less. It sounds good and it reads well but, frankly, it is a purely cosmetic operation as far as the consumer is concerned.
I thought I would go over the list of legislation in the two provinces to which I referred, Ontario and Alberta. In Ontario, the first is the personal property security act. These are all in the Revised Statutes of 1970; I do not know when they may have been passed in their original form. Then there
November 3, 1976

is the credit unions act, the mechanics liens act, the conditional sales act, the loan and trust corporations act, the consumer protection act and the bills of sale and chattel mortgages act. In the province of Alberta there is, as I recall, the judicature act, the mortgage brokers' regulation act (1964), the direct sales calculation act (1966), and the credit and loan agreements act (1967). There are any number of parts to that act, one which from the consumer's point of view is a real refuge. It is said that some provinces are havens for the absconding debtor, the person who buys on time and then wants to beat it.
On the other hand, do you not agree, Mr. Speaker, that business losses incurred when customers do not pay their debts must be recovered at other points in the operation if the company concerned is to stay in business? This is what happens when, for example, an automobile dealer makes a loss in connection with a car he has repossessed or when one of his debtors absconds. Such losses have to be taken into consideration in the course of other transactions, otherwise the dealer will go under.
The situation is the same for a furniture dealer, a radio and television dealer-any type of store or business operation which operates on credit. If things are made too easy for the so-called poor borrower or poor purchaser, one of two consequences will ensue. Either the business will become more discriminating in granting credit, thereby narrowing the field for borrowers-an effect which is counterproductive to the bill before us-or losses will be such that additional costs will be placed on the shoulders of consumers. There is nothing like sharing the load! Again, I submit that this is counterproductive to the spirit of this legislation.
Society certainly has the right to ask that when there is a transaction all relevant information should be clearly stated. In the case, say, of the purchase of a refrigerator, the cash price of the unit in question should be stated. So should the price with trade-in, if a trade-in is involved. Then there will be the dates and the amounts and number of regular payments, payments which may be blended so as to include interest, or calculated on the basis of a declining amount of interest, leaving a balance to become payable on such and such a date. To the amount to be paid there would be added the cost of a credit report, if it is part of the transaction, as well as the cost of insuring the purchaser, if such were part of the contract. Registration charges, if required by provincial law, would also be listed and, finally, the total cost.
Having arrived at that figure, it is simple to take the cash price of the product, subtract it from the total cost and arrive, by simple mathematics, at the cost of borrowing, the cost of the transaction. It is spread over so many months. I do not underestimate the capacity of a purchaser who buys a refrigerator to understand the type of contract in which this is spelled out. Incidentally, there are many provinces in which a person buying under such a contract has the right to go back within, say, five business days and say that he is sorry, he has changed his mind. I do not see that provision in this bill, but it may be the answer sometimes to the practices of some pretty high pressure salesmanship. Salesmen of home appliances, automo-
Proteclion of Borrowers and Depositors biles, radio and televisions are pretty skilled. They have to be; theirs is a highly competitive world. Take the case of a purchaser who cannot afford to buy. He goes back home, talks to his wife and says, "What were we thinking about? Buying this is absolutely crazy". Having reflected on the matter, he can go back and say to the salesman, "I am sorry; we have changed our minds".
That, Mr. Speaker, is the ultimate protection and I am quite prepared to see that here. When it comes to the purchase of an automobile, every blessed cent of the cost of that vehicle which will go into every monthly payment should be listed in appropriate columns-no fine print so small one almost needs a magnifying glass to read it-so the figures are there in tabular form before the purchaser, readily explainable to him or her. That I would agree with, and it is provided for in some provinces.
Are we going to see such provisions as this in the regulations, Mr. Speaker? My colleagues have expressed some concern about the regulations, and I hope the minister will break with tradition and disclose the regulations during the committee hearings. After all, this is not a bill that was dreamed up two weeks ago and is being rushed through; we have been hearing about it over eons of time almost. I am sure the department has had every opportunity for consultation and examination of provincial legislation which has preceded this measure by up to 20 years. I have before me a copy of a letter dated October 20 from the Consumers' Association of Canada which raises some points of query about which there is legitimate argument.
My final point, Mr. Speaker, has to do with loan-sharking. It sounds great to say that there are going to be penalties imposed on loan sharks. But it is not so much the loan-sharking that is the bad thing; it is the coercion and the efforts at extortion today that are so reprehensible. These are the offences of which people are convicted.
Does anyone in their right mind believe that there is going to be a written agreement between a lender and a borrower who enter into a transaction on, say, the docks in Montreal, where there has been evidence of loan-sharking? What about a transaction that takes place on some construction sites, where judicial inquiries have elicited that loan-sharking has been carried on by various individuals both inside and outside the industrial personnel? Will there be any agreement between gamblers and among the underworld where this type of operation known as loan-sharking takes place? Do you think, Mr. Speaker, that an agreement will be signed between a lender who is going to put up, say, a couple of thousand dollars for some poor fool who has gambled away that much money with a bookie, and that enforcers will collect this loan? What if he says, "No, I am not going to pay; you take me to court?" What will happen to him will be the baseball bat across his legs and arms. That is what happens under loan-sharking.
I say that combating loan-sharking is no function of a bill of this type. Give the police the authority to deal with loan

Protection of Borrowers and Depositors sharks. Put it in the Criminal code where it belongs. Then we will not have to go through all this nonsense of talking about agreements and civil recourse. In that league, Mr. Speaker, there is no civil recourse. Where does one imagine so-called loan-sharking is carried on? There may be usurious loan practices carried on at times among some pawnbrokers, but in such cases what was the purpose of the loan? Was it necessary to pay the rent or to buy food? Not all of those transactions is so, shall I say, humdrum and for such a useful purpose, not by a long chalk. Such transactions usually are on the wrong side of the law or for some purpose that cannot stand examination by the light of day. Let us put this kind of activity under the Criminal Code. I hope we can persuade the minister that he should try to persuade his colleague, the Attorney General, to include appropriate provisions in the bill that is to follow what was Bill C-83.
We should send this bill to committee. The principle of it is to amend certain acts. We are going to repeal the Small Loans Act and do a number of other things, but the principle of the whole bill is to amend certain acts. That is fine; I am quite agreeable to it and the bill should be sent to committee. Outside of that though, Mr. Speaker, I think this is a very cosmetic bill which will not accomplish the purpose the minister has set out for it.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin by commending the new Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Abbott) for bringing forward this bill as his initial piece of legislation on entering the cabinet. I think he has established a legitimate beachhead from which to launch his ministry. We may well disagree with some points in the legislation, but we certainly agree on the necessity for it. I hope he will be open-minded enough to listen to what members have to say during second reading debate, that he will listen to the proposals that are made, and gather together some of the hints that members offer relative to the amendments that he should expect at committee stage and at report stage.
I hope he will be open-minded enough to realize that even the best minister cannot bring forward perfect legislation, and that it is not a sign of weakness to allow amendments later on, but a sign of strength. Again I congratulate him for bringing forward this piece of legislation. It is his responsibility to act on behalf of the public to protect either the unwary or the defenceless, and not to encourage or reward unrestrained impulse buying.
The kind of legislation we are discussing lends itself to the creation of many victims in the marketplace. The very term "consumer", which is part of the title of the minister's portfolio, gives us some hint as to what the marketplace thinks of the ordinary individual. He is no longer a person or a human being; he is now completely depersonalized and is simply a consumer. The term has obviously been invented by some unfeeling genius of the market system whose responsibility it is to provide devourers of the unending array and supply of

gadgets spewed out by the industries which have hired these callous hawkers of the marketplace. It is not the responsibility of the minister to encourage that kind of depersonalization in the marketplace. Rather, it is his responsibility to humanize the whole process by which we buy and sell.
The bill sets out the responsibilities of a lender and puts on him the onus to disclose certain very important information, such as the total amount of the loan being discussed, the total amount of repayment, the dollar amount of interest per annum, the effective annual percentage rate, the amounts and rates of payments to be made to the lender or to a designated third party, the conditions regarding payment of penalties and the computation of the same, and the effective date of the beginning of the transaction.
It has been said that the only thing money cannot buy is poverty. I suppose at one time that was true, but in the market place and in the marketing system today that is already becoming a contradiction because of the ready availability of debt or finance. Indeed, today money can buy poverty.
I would like to address myself for a few minutes to the whole business of consumer finance as it relates to the credit card system. I do not suppose there is a member in this House who does not use a credit card; they are a very convenient way of buying.

The hon. member says he cannot get one. I suppose he cannot pass the character test. Perhaps he has come to the point, as other people have, where obviously his credit must be good because he owes everybody. However, in all seriousness I think anybody who can resist the pressure to borrow is to be commended.
I was talking to the minister just today about the fact that there is too much pressure on the public to apply for credit cards. There is unending pressure through television ads, magazines end even the mail service. At the present time the post office is operating, but it is strange that credit is now possible even through provincial schemes. Where the credit card companies get their mailing lists, I do not know. It would be interesting to find out. The fact that a credit card company can mail out credit cards or applications for credit cards is something which deserves serious examination by the government. It seems that consumers face no relief from the endless barrage of credit card companies saying how easy it is to borrow and how good and how convenient it is. We see happy young people pictured flicking out credit cards and making purchases, but there is never any mention that the rate of interest is 18 per cent or 24 per cent.
We see these people walk away in ecstasy, but we do not see them getting their statements at the end of the month or
November 3, 1976

paying usurious interest rates. I think the government has a responsibility to put a curb on this pressure which is always facing the consumer. I know we are not dealing with such things as subliminal advertising, but the private citizen no longer seems to have the freedom of independent decision. He is being pressured and conned into making decisions and he is caught off guard. I know we cannot endure a "buyer beware" market, nor can the government be paternalistic in this sense and protect the public from all the pitfalls there may be, but I think the government has some responsibility and should have these companies exercise restraint in this area.
Just last week when I was home I went through some of my mail and came across a letter from Master Charge. I do not even have a Master Charge card, but that letter in effect said, "Congratulations, it is now possible for you to borrow up to a limit of $1,500". I never even asked for that privilege. These companies are inviting people to go into debt. The government has a responsibility to put pressure on such companies to restrict that kind of advertising.
The government is taking away the percentage limits the lending companies can impose on their borrowers. The government says that if it puts loan-sharks out of the market-which is a happy thought, if it can be done-then taking away the ceiling on lending rates will simply make the market more competitive. I am not convinced that that is true. That could be the case, but I am not convinced. However, if the government is going to take away that ceiling, it certainly ought to take a very close look at the number of dollars these companies are spending in advertising to convince the public that it ought to use their credit, just as I think we ought to look at the amount of advertising used in other industries to convince shoppers that their product is best.
Why should General Motors have a multimillion dollar advertising budget to convince me that 1 should buy a General Motors' car? Surely most people know whether they want a GM, Chrysler, Ford, American Motors' or any other kind of vehicle. We do not have to be convinced by that kind of advertising, and the same is true with regard to credit. If the government is going to take the restraints off the lending market by taking away the interest ceiling, it also has a responsibility to consider the amount of money credit card companies are spending on advertising.
I thought we had an excellent presentation before the House last night by the hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray). I believe he spoke from a very informed position, since he is a former minister of consumer and corporate affairs. I thought he gave a very responsible and well thought-out presentation regarding this legislation. The criticisms he had for the bill were not vitriolic; they were constructive. He pointed out the gaps in the legislation and offered alternative proposals which the government might introduce if it wants to improve this legislation.
I want to emphasize that the minister would display his strength as a minister if he had the courage to entertain the
Protection of Borrowers and Depositors kinds of amendments that will be suggested during this debate and at the committee stage. The hon. member for Windsor West said, as recorded at page 704 of Hansard'.
However, this bill does nothing to ensure that the low income borrower who has in the past found it difficult to obtain credit from legitimate institutions, will not continue to be forced into the hands of loan sharks rather than getting that credit from legitimate lenders. The bill does nothing to ensure that the borrower, who found it difficult in the past to get credit except from companies licensed under the Small Loans Act, will, when this bill is passed, get credit on terms as favourable as those now provided for loans under the act, either from small loan companies or other credit granting institutions. The minister in his speech on second reading said at one point:
"That is why we propose the repeal of the Small Loans Act. Instead we are proposing a strong and comprehensive set of protective devices applicable to all forms and levels of consumer credit so that consumers will be assured of access to loans bearing fair and reasonable credit charges."
It is a truism among the people who have to go to the lending market, to the regular financial institutions to borrow money, that the only time money will be lent to them is when they can prove that they really do not need it. That is another way of saying that one needs so much collateral that one probably could get along very well without borrowing the money unless one wanted to expand his enterprise. The fact is that some of the lending institutions are so careful in establishing their criteria and in examining their prospective clients that it becomes very difficult to borrow money from them.
A friend of mine went to his local bank. He wanted to do some renovations to his house. I think he was a school teacher; at least, he seemed to be a very respected person in the community. He had good credentials but he simply did not have too many resources, as is the case with most teachers. This man went to his banker and said he wanted to borrow "X" number of dollars for the purpose of renovating his house. After discussion the banker said that he did not think he could do that for him because he did not have very much collateral. They made small-talk for a while and when my friend went to leave, the banker, in the usual closing remarks said, "any time I can do something for you, please come and see me". My friend said that the time was then.
The fact is that these institutions tend to be so secretive and security-oriented that only the most prosperous clients stand a chance of getting the kind of terms they need in respect of loans. As the hon. member for Windsor West pointed out, if you do not have blue chip kind of credit, it is not likely that you will get that kind of loan. So a person who might in every other sense qualify for this type of credit, eventually ends up going to the loan-sharking business.
The minister proposes to do away with loan-sharking. I hope he is successful. I hope that this bill makes it possible. However, human nature being what it is, and because of the unscrupulousness of the people already engaged in that kind of business, I am not inclined to be sanguine about- the hope. Because of the very nature of these people, who are dangerous and usurious, they will continue to operate in a devious fashion and there will always be a market for their product. They will simply go further underground. The borrower who does not have blue chip collateral will end up in some kind of financial arrangement like this.
