Protection of Borrowers and Depositors
The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) asked, what is the recourse? The bill says the recourse is the law and that the lender will have to prove before the law that the rates are not usurious or criminal. That kind of lender has other ways of handling his client who would have the temerity to go before the law. There is the matter of the baseball bat, the slashed tires or the threatening phone calls at three o'clock in the morning. These unscrupulous people take matters into their own hands. Their method is intimidation. So what is the borrower to do in this kind of situation? If, in normal circumstances, he has good credit but cannot borrow at an ordinary lending institution, what is he to do?
I suggest the hon. member for Windsor West came up with a very reasonable solution which I think deserves examination by all members of the House, certainly by the members of the committee and the minister. As recorded at page 706 of Hansard, the hon. member said:
A simple approach would be to require the licensing, the registration, of all moneylenders not subject to be licensed under other federal or provincial laws. One can agree that duplication of licensing is not necessary. But why remove even the requirement for licensing from those now subject to it under the existing law? Whatever may be said for the authority to be given to the new administrator under the act, that authority is not to exercise a licensing jurisdiction.
The simple solution is a licensing requirement. This government, of all governments, ought to have some kind of experience in licensing. When we think of the government's proposal in respect of Bill C-83, one would think with that kind of reflex action the government would have thought of that proposal when it came to the matter of moneylenders.
I understand that the government of British Columbia has brought forward legislation which requires moneylenders in British Columbia to be licensed. What is wrong with that? Why not take the people who want to be involved in the moneylending business and require that they take a course of study which would prepare them for this kind of business? During that course of study the licensing process would soon eliminate people who are not equipped to be involved in this kind of business. We have this situation in other areas. It happens in the insurance business. To be a reputable insurance salesman a man must pass a course; then he is given a licence to sell insurance.
We do it in the real estate business. Banks have to be licensed. It seems to me that the hon. member for Windsor West has come up with a very legitimate proposal for the government to examine and to bring forward in committee. The government should let it be examined in amendment form. I do not know why the government should not want to adopt this suggestion. One of their own members brought it forward. It seems to me that it deserves examination.
This whole business of pressure to buy, pressure to borrow, has very invidious dimensions. I have already mentioned the credit card business and consumer orientation, but when you see how the marketplace operates today where, for example, large department stores also become lending institutions for one who is buying their merchandise, it takes you back to the

company store, "Sixteen stone, and what do you get? Another day older and deeper in debt." We have examples of large, chain department stores charging what may be a legitimate mark-up on their merchandise, but they are making another 18 per cent to 24 per cent on the money they lend to the consumer who purchases from them.
That kind of vertical organization lends itself to a lot of abuse. I am not saying that the chains we have in Canada are abusing the system; I am saying the system lends itself to abuse. Then you have a company such as the Power Corporation, for example, which is an enterprise involved in transportation, in communications, in advertising and in moneylending.

speechtext: Also, in politics.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REGULATE INTEREST ON JUDGMENT DEBTS AND AMEND CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext:
You have those kinds of relationships. We have to get away from the pressure on the consumer encouraging him, almost forcing him, into impulse buying. Let me get back to the borrower who comes to the lending market with what would be classed, I suppose, as secondary qualifications to borrow money. The present legislation says there is the litigation process which he can go through if he feels he is being charged too much. On the surface, it sounds reasonable-the lender now has to justify the rates he is charging. But it seems to me, if I understand the bill correctly, that that is after the fact. After they have engaged in an agreement and the borrower realizes that he is being charged more than he should be charged, it is then his prerogative to go before a judge and engage in litigation.
However, in so many cases the very people who become victims of this kind of money market are those who are not accustomed to going before the law; they cannot afford it. They are not accustomed to going before the law because they are not in that kind of world, and they do not have that kind of income to hire a lawyer or even to get legal advice. While the proposal seems to be legitimate, I am afraid that it will break down and the very people whom the legislation is designed to help will continue to be the victims because they have a fear of the legal system, they stay away from the courts and they are not accustomed to being in that kind of position.
The hon. member for Windsor West said that the criminal rate of interest for which sanctions will apply to the institutions, transactions to be exempted from the act, and the kind of information to be spelled out in the advertising in which credit is mentioned cause him concern. He said the government must table a complete set of draft regulations with the committee studying the bill. He hit the point right on the head. We have had too much exposure to legislation which provides that regulations will come at a later date or will be drafted after the legislation has been passed. We have experienced that, especially with Bill C-83. We faced it in immigration laws where the government could change the regulations overnight and simply impose them on the public without providing the people with prior information.
The hon. member for Windsor West has a very strong point. He said there can be no meaningful parliamentary debate, nor can there be meaningful public input as to the content of the
November 3, 1976

bill without these regulations being put before us at the earliest possible date which, he says, should not be later than the beginning of the committee hearings. 1 should like to encourage the minister to draft those regulations and give himself that much time before he moves forward with this legislation, so that the committee can examine the regulations and provide the kind of input that the legislation needs if we are to do the best we can for the public.
If we do not have the best kind of bill issuing from this debate and from discussion in committee, only the public will suffer. The very people whom the minister wants to help will be hurt the most. The tragedy is that the people will have confidence in this legislation, but that confidence will be betrayed if the minister does not submit it for scrutiny. I encourage the minister to give himself more time so that the regulations can be drafted and presented to the committee. We should allow amendments to come forward and let the public benefit from the best possible discussion and scrutiny of this legislation so that we will get the best protection that the public deserves under it.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REGULATE INTEREST ON JUDGMENT DEBTS AND AMEND CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to take part in this very important debate on Bill C-16, an act to provide for the protection of borrowers and depositors, to regulate interest on judgment debts, to repeal the Interest Act, the Pawnbrokers Act and the Small Loans Act and to amend certain other statutes in consequence thereof. I am afraid we are off to a very bad start with Bill C-16, as the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) stated. It is similar to Bill C-83, which was very poorly drafted. If it ever comes back, which we hope it will not, about 100 amendments will be presented to try to improve the bill.
The Globe and Mail of October 29 reported the Canadian Bankers' Association as saying that this bill, rather than achieving the stated objective of eliminating unnecessary complexities and confusion in the credit field, in its present form could confuse and dislocate consumer finance to the detriment of all Canadians. It reported that the CBA has serious reservations as to the contents of the bill in the form in which it has been introduced, saying it appears that rather than meeting specifically Canadian needs, based on Canadian experience and the need to operate within the Canadian institutional framework, foreign precedents and procedures have been adopted. It claimed that as the bill stands, the cost and availability of credit to consumers would be adversely affected since legitimate lenders would face difficulties in their administration and assets and liabilities management. It noted that another stated objective of the bill is to rationalize federal credit legislation, saying that with this the bill attempts to cover such a diverse range of topics as consumer credit, mortgages, deposits, advertising and disclosure, without having regard to existing federal and provincial legislation.
The newspaper noted that the CBA argues the public would have been better served, and more effective and useful legisla-
Protection of Borrowers and Depositors tion would have emerged more quickly, if the government had allowed for adequate public discussion of the proposals before the introduction of the legislation, perhaps through a white paper process. The report continued that the CBA said after it has had an opportunity to study the bill it will prepare detailed alternative submissions for parliamentary committees to consider.
On November 1, the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) put the following question to the minister:
I hesitate to interrupt the minister, Mr. Speaker, but I wonder if by the time he completes his explanation on this point he could tell me how he believes he can lump together charges under provincial legislation for the registration of chattel mortgages or other forms of incumbencies with interest charges that are to the benefit of the lender. Those are two different things. I should like to know how the minister believes he can lump together apples, oranges, cherries, bananas and other things in the same basket and come out with common interest charges and rates.
The minister replied:
I would prefer not to attempt to answer that question because it opens the problems of provincial instruments-
That indicates how ill-prepared the government was and how poorly the bill is drafted. Under a heading "Loan bill constitutionality queried", an article in the Montreal Gazette of November 2 refers to the hon. member for Brome-Missis-squoi (Mr. Grafftey), saying:
-he has doubts about the constitutionality of a government bill aimed at halting loan-sharking and protecting borrowers from unfair interest rates.
The article goes on to say that the hon. member doubted there had been full consultation with the provinces before the bill was introduced. Mr. Speaker, this is evidence of complete lack of consultation, and now we doubt if the bill is even constitutional. Now let us look at some clauses of the bill, Mr. Speaker. Clause 2 (2) (a) reads:
Where the payment is in the form of an amount paid that is sent by mail to the lender at his latest known mailing address and, on the day it is sent, the payment is in a form that is negotiable by the lender, on that day-
With the mail service, we have, Mr. Speaker, that clause could cause very serious problems and will have to be looked at in committee. Clause 33 reads as follows:
Where, in any proceedings in relation to a particular lending transaction, a dispute arises as to whether a payment by a borrower under the transaction was made on or before the day on or before which such payment was, under the terms of the lending transaction, required to be made, such payment shall, in the absence of any evidence to the contrary, be presumed to have been made on or before that day.
I do not know how this is to be recorded. I would imagine lenders will have to photostat all letters. I will be interested to hear them explain, when they appear before the committee, how they will carry out this provision. On the matter of the obligations of lenders, clauses 17 and 18 provide that all lenders shall maintain records and books of account which would enable the administrator to identify credit charges in individual transactions. These records shall be kept by the lender until such time as prescribed by regulation. Here we get into the question of the regulations. This matter has been mentioned by other members during the debate.
It is puzzling to see how all the regulations can be administered, when little bombshells are dropped from time to time.

The bill says that the records may then be destroyed; a lender shall provide a periodic statement of account to a borrower without charge; frequency and form will be specified by regulation; upon the payment of a fee in an amount to be specified by regulation, the lender shall provide to the borrower an interim statement of account. All these procedures should be stated in the bill and not by regulation, Mr. Speaker.
Because of the considerable dependence of this section on unrevealed regulations, analysis of it would not be fruitful. However, the extent of the use of regulations is itself significant. Why, for instance, the length of time the records must be kept should be at the discretion of the governor in council is an interesting question. On the matter of depositors, clauses 19 to 21 state that a deposit is defined as the aggregate of moneys, including interest, accepted or held by the institution in return for which the institution is primarily liable, for which it must issue a receipt and give credit to the depositor's account. To retain the character of a deposit the institution must also be obligated to repay the moneys on demand or on notice.
Advertisements shall not claim to provide a deposit interest payment, except as provided by regulation; the amount of interest earned shall be calculated in the manner prescribed by regulation; the frequency with which interest is credited to accounts shall be monthly, or at such more frequent intervals as may be prescribed by regulation; all deposit-taking institutions shall disclose to the depositor the annual rate on the applicable class of deposits, the method by which that interest is calculated and such other information as may be prescribed by regulation. Mr. Speaker, we will have a longer list of regulations than there are clauses in the bill. These sections apply to all deposit-taking institutions except to classes of institutions that are exempted by regulation.
Emphasis has been placed on the words "by regulation" because of the magnitude of what these sections will regulate. In chartered banks, trust companies and mortgage loan companies alone there are over $40 billion of savings deposits. That discretionary powers over the treatment of such an enormous amount of money should be proposed at all is a frightening thought. A further source of alarm is that control over transactions involving this amount of money is vested in the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, a department that has no mandate to concern itself with the stability of the monetary system.
A possible scenario where these deposit provisions could interfere with monetary stability is here outlined. Assuming that the regulations will specify that interest payments are to be calculated daily, it will become more profitable for depositors to use chequing and non-chequing savings accounts rather than personal chequing accounts which bear no interest. There will thus be a shift from demand deposits to notice deposits. In terms of the classifications used by the Bank of Canada, funds will shift from M-l, currency and demand deposits, to M-2, currency and privately-held deposits, including savings deposits and non-personal term and notice deposits. Since the Bank of Canada fastens upon M-l as the principal method of regulating the size of the monetary mass, to the extent that

funds move from M-l to M-2 Bank of Canada control is reduced.
Further, chartered banks currently must maintain reserves of 12 per cent on demand deposits and 4 per cent on notice deposits. If funds shift from demand to notice deposits, a reduction in the aggregate level of reserves maintained by the banks will occur. This would not only reduce Bank of Canada control of the money supply but would also release large quantities of funds into the monetary system. The above scenario is not meant to suggest that this will occur but that it might. Surely, there should be a requirement that any regulations proposed for deposits by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs should be first checked and approved by the Department of Finance and or the Bank of Canada.
Although these sections leave much of their substance to regulation, yet a further point can be made. Inasmuch as Canada savings bonds are available only to consumers, it should be incumbent upon the government of Canada to lead the way in interest rate disclosure by agreeing to treat Canada savings bonds in the same manner as deposit-taking institutions are required to treat interest on non-chequing deposits.
I now come to the powers of the administrator, dealt with in clauses 24 to 30, inclusive. The administrator shall keep a register about lenders which is likely to be of interest to borrowers, including judicial proceedings, under the BDPA or any federal or provincial statute. Borrowers, upon payment of a fee, may inspect the register or obtain a certificate of compliance concerning the lender's activities. The bill states that the administrator may require a lender to submit information regarding lending transactions. Also, the administrator may enter the premises of the lender at reasonable times, examine or audit his books, obtain assistance in his examination from the lender and, if it appears to the administrator that an offence has been committed, seize all relevant information. Entry can only be approved by a judge, and only when a complaint has been received from a borrower.
Information obtained in this manner is privileged and may only be made public in enforcing the act. The power of the administrator is considerable but is protected from abuse by the requirement that judicial authorization shall be sought in advance of the use of any extraordinary remedies. If it is granted that the strictures specified in the act are necessary and beneficial, then it is apparent that a person must be vested with the power to apply them. In one area, however, the administrator has power that may be abused and for which there is no judicial authorization required.
The administrator shall keep a register which will include any information which, in the judgment of the administrator, is likely to be of use to the borrower. This information will include records of judicial proceedings against lenders, whether under the BDPA or any other act. The legislation does not specify whether these records of court proceedings only will include cases in which the lender has been found guilty. Failure to limit the judgment of the administrator in this way
November 3, 1976

could allow the administrator to conduct a campaign of innuendo against a lender by simply listing the actions brought against a lender whether or not they were successful.
1 now deal with clauses 37 to 40. inclusive, which have to do with offences. Persons who demand an excessive credit charge, unlawfully destroy records or accounts or employ any threat or coercion against a borrower, are liable, on summary conviction, to a fine of between $1,000 and $10,000 and/or to imprisonment for two years or, upon indictment, to a fine not less than $1,000 and to imprisonment for five years. Illegal types of threat or coercion are identified. They include: intent to use violence, threat of public accusation, threat of sale or assignment, threat of arrest or seizure of possessions. Activities which constitute threatening are identified: use of obscene language, placement of anonymous telephone calls, collect calls or calls at inconvenient times.
The purpose of the very detailed list of illegal practices is to prohibit practices used by loan sharks or unscrupulous lenders in obtaining payment. But since practices of intimidation or of abusive conduct or of threat or coercion are already deemed criminal offences under the Criminal Code, it is unlikely that this bill will create any new deterrent to criminal acts. The problem is one of enforcement rather than of law.
May I now make some general comments. Much of the borrowers and depositors protection bill will be of considerable benefit to consumers who borrow or deposit, and is not likely to impose an undue financial or administrative burden on the various classes of financial institutions which either lend or accept deposits. Certain features of the bill, however, are manifestly unfair to lenders and, indeed, may be counterproductive for consumers. Implementation of the legislation in its current form may disrupt loan markets to the extent that funds available to borrowers through legal sources will be reduced. Other sections of the bill may only serve to confuse consumers, when the object is to allow them to be better informed. For depositors, benefits are not clear at this time, as most of the procedures by which interest on deposits is to be advertised, computed and credited will be prescribed by regulation.
Few would dispute that new legislation in this area is required. The principal federal borrower protection laws are the Interest Act and the Small Loans Act, last amended in 1917 and 1956 respectively. It is clear that many significant changes in the financial system have occurred since these times, including a much greater willingness of consumers to borrow, much higher general interest rates, greater sophistication in advertising, the large-scale entry of chartered banks into the consumer loan market, and a proliferation in the range of financial services available to consumers.
Bringing the act up to date, however, is not the only change required. The Small Loans Act only regulates designated moneylenders and loan companies. There are many other classes of financial institutions, not the least being the banks, which are not affected by the provisions of this legislation. Provincial governments have implemented some legislation which is of assistance to borrowers, but these protections have
Protection of Borrowers and Depositors neither been complete in their coverage nor consistent between provinces.
Bill C-16 proposes protection that will be uniform in degree throughout the country and will affect all institutions which lend to consumers or closely-held corporations. The Interest Act will be repealed and replaced by one piece of legislation. At the same time, responsibility for administration of the act will be vested in a different minister. Although there was no privy councillor assigned to administer the Interest Act, it was assumed to be under the general authority of the minister of finance of the day and in practice required no administrative guidance, being used primarily by the courts. Administration of the Small Loans Act is the responsibility of the minister of finance of the day. The new BDPA will be administered by the minister of consumer and corporate affairs.
This change in administration itself raises some questions which may be of some importance. The objective of the BDPA is to protect consumer borrowers and depositors. The objective of the Department of Finance in administering small loans legislation is not only to ensure the propriety of management policies and operations of small loans companies but also to ensure their financial solvency. Further, the Department of Finance is charged with maintaining an orderly financial system. It is possible that the goals of borrower and depositor protection may conflict with those of the financial solvency of loan companies or of an orderly financial system. Since it is within the mandate of the Department of Finance to examine policies proposed by other departments and agencies of government having an effect on economic or financial conditions, it may be useful to direct questions to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) as to the likely impact of the BDPA legislation.
I said a moment ago that the BDPA intends to provide national standards of protection. Thus, where a provincial statute is in conflict with a federal one it appears that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs intends that the federal act shall be supreme. This presumption of jurisdiction is based on a constitutional premise. Section 91(19) of the BNA Act indicates that matters pertaining to interest are within federal power. Federal reasoning is that "all transactions where interest is involved must therefore be considered to be within federal jurisdiction."
This interpretation may seem to be sound, but is suspect for two reasons. First, in this bill the definition of "interest" is often extended somewhat beyond its original 1867 meaning, as when "credit charge rate" is used in place of the notion of interest rate and is only defined precisely by regulation. Second, although a loan or deposit is a transaction where interest is involved, the bill regulates aspects of a loan or deposit transaction which have little or nothing to do with interest, as when late or early penalty payment procedures are specified, when loan account statements are demanded or when unacceptable collection procedures are designated. Rules in all these areas may be desirable, but the federal jurisdiction-

Protection of Borrowers and Depositors al power of interest is being stretched in interpretation when it is used as justification for regulation of these practices. Objections from provinces may be expected.
A rather alarming number of the provisions of Bill C-16 are deliberately vague. Details will be filled in by regulation. In a bill of 44 clauses there are at least 20 distinct cases where clarification as to the meaning of terms or the procedures to be followed will be given in regulations which will be proclaimed by the governor in council. The only check on the unrestrained power to make regulations is the provision in clause 31(2) which requires that an opportunity to hear representations shall be provided to interested parties.
Many of the regulations will specify matters of substance rather than of detail. Examples of definitional or procedural matters which will be revealed by regulation include, (1) the definitions of "credit charge rate", "lowest rate quoted" for prime or non-chequing rates, and "variable rate" of a loan, and (2) the procedures to be followed in advertising credit availability, making full disclosure of the cost of a loan, providing statements of account to borrowers-manner, form and periodicity-advertising, calculating and crediting interest on deposits. Application for so many discretionary powers in a bill should give cause for concern in itself, but the extent of the powers sought is quite astounding. The bill proposes to give unchallengeable power to the governor in council to control the manner and form in which billions of dollars of deposits and loans are made every year. Whether such power would be used wisely is a question which pales into insignificance beside the question of whether such unchallengeable power should exist at all.
I now wish to deal with the principal provisions of the bill. The interest rate ceilings are removed in clause 3. Apart from restrictions imposed by this and other acts of parliament, any rate of interest may be charged "that is agreed upon." This provision constitutes the removal of the interest rate ceilings imposed by the Small Loans Act. Under that act a rate of interest could not be charged on a loan that would exceed, (a) 2 per cent per month on any unpaid balance less than $300, (b) 1 per cent per month on any unpaid balance over $300 but less than $1,000, or (c) one-half of 1 per cent per month on any unpaid balance exceeding $1,000 but less than $1,500. Longer term loans were subject to even lower rates.
The removal of interest rate ceilings is a source of benefit to both lenders and consumers. The ceilings were imposed at a time when general interest rates were at a much lower level. Under more recent conditions, where a loan company has had to pay rates in excess of 11 per cent to purchase the money it loans, it is impossible to expect loan companies to lend at rates of 12 per cent and less and still remain solvent. Under certain conditions, for certain amounts of money, a loan company would have been expected to lend at rates less than those offered by chartered banks exempt from small loans legislation which have, because of superior leverage and lower costs of raising funds, a much lower cost of doing business. Such a situation causes moneylenders and small loan companies to turn down all but the most credit-worthy borrowers or to lend

amounts above the regulatory coverage of the act, which is $1,500.
Loan companies affected by rate regulation have generally been opposed to it. They have argued that rate regulation is unnecessary. They say:
The degree of competition among various credit suppliers and among the member companies of our own industry guarantees the vast majority of borrowers that adequate credit will be available to them at fair, efficient and competitive rates.
This was contained in a submission by the Canadian Consumer Loan Association to the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. The CCLA is now part of the Association of Canadian Financial Corporations. Consumers will be satisfied in one respect, that loans will be more freely available to borrowers. However, the Consumers' Association of Canada maintains that the retention of a graduated rate ceiling of up to $7,500 is still necessary, arguing that the competitive rate model is "theoretical" only, particularly for low income and or sophisticated borrowers. They recognize that rate regulation may deprive high-risk borrowers of access to credit, but if the problem of the high-risk borrower can only be salved by giving him access to high-cost credit, this is not, in our view, an objectionable effect. Although explicit rate regulation is removed by this clause, control over rates exists in another section, clause 8. To a certain extent, then, rate regulation appears in a more flexible though not necessarily a more satisfactory form.
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
